subject: Science
board: KS3 National Curriculum via Pearson Exploring Science, building to Edexcel International GCSE Biology, Chemistry and Physics
source: School Science curriculum journey 2026–27 (Year 7 Term 1: 7A Cells, tissues, organs and systems; 7E Mixtures and separation) and the school's Pearson 5-year Biology and Chemistry schemes (Exploring Science topics 7Aa–7Ae, 7Ea–7Ee) and 7E assessments; practicals adapted for live online lessons; INSET lesson standard.

lessons.title: Life processes: what makes something alive?
lessons.bigQuestion: Is a car alive? It moves, uses fuel and gives out waste.
objectives: Use the life processes to decide whether something is alive
Explain why one process alone is not enough
successCriteria: Name the seven life processes (MRS GREN)
Classify things as living, dead or never alive with reasons
Argue why a car or a crystal is not alive using several processes
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: life as a gift from Allah (Al-Hayy, the Ever-Living); English: building an argument
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at the complexity of living things; moral: respect for all life

keywords.def: a living thing
the seven things all living organisms do
releasing energy from food inside cells
getting rid of waste made by the body
sensing and responding to changes in the surroundings

starter: Bismillah. Name three living things you saw today
Is fire alive? Write yes or no with one reason
What do plants need to grow?

teach.heading: MRS GREN
bullets: Every living thing does all seven
One or two are not enough
teach.note: Introduce each process with an example from a human and a plant. Ask: 'How does a plant move?' (Leaves turn to the light; roots grow down.)

head: Letter
Process
Example
rows: a sunflower turning to the Sun
pulling your hand from a hot pan

teach.heading: Living, dead or never alive?
bullets: Never alive: never did all seven
teach.note: Sort: a wooden chair (dead: was a tree), a stone (never alive), a mushroom (living), a leaf on the ground (dead).

teach.heading: Is a car alive?
bullets: But it cannot grow, reproduce or sense
teach.note: Answer the big question as a class debate. Push for evidence: 'Which processes are missing?'

misconception.wrong: It moves, so it is alive
misconception.right: An organism must carry out all seven life processes

teach.heading: Excretion or egestion?
bullets: Excretion: waste made by cells (CO₂, urea)
Egestion: undigested food leaving the body
teach.note: Stretch point: faeces are egested, not excreted, because the food never entered our cells.

teach.heading: Check: life processes
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A crystal grows larger in a salt solution. Why is it NOT alive?
options: It only shows growth, not all seven processes
check.why: Living things must carry out all seven processes. A crystal grows but does not respire, reproduce, excrete or feed.

practice: Write the seven life processes using MRS GREN
Is a seed alive? Explain using two life processes
Give one example of sensitivity in a plant
independent: Core: Sort ten objects (apple, robot, bacterium, cotton T-shirt, fish, candle flame, tree, coal, virus, cat) into living, dead, never alive
Extend: Explain why a candle flame seems alive, using three life processes it appears to show and three it lacks
Stretch: Scientists debate whether viruses are alive. Use the life processes to argue both sides in a short paragraph.
exit: What does the S in MRS GREN stand for?
Is a wooden spoon dead or never alive?
Give one reason a robot is not alive.
lessons.homework: Find five things at home and classify each as living, dead or never alive, giving one life process as evidence.
lessons.send: Support: MRS GREN picture cards. EAL: process words with images. Stretch: viruses debate.

lessons.title: Organs and what they do
lessons.bigQuestion: Which organ could you live without, and which could you not?
objectives: Recall the main human and plant organs
Describe the function of each organ
successCriteria: Name and locate major human organs
Match organs to their functions, including plant organs
Explain how two organs work together for one life process
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: heart and lungs in exercise; PSHE: organ donation decisions
lessons.smsc: Moral: organ donation and different views on it, including Islamic scholarly views

keywords.def: a structure made of different tissues working together to do a job
the job something does
organ that pumps blood around the body
plant organ that makes food by photosynthesis

starter: Name a part of a plant

teach.heading: Human organs
bullets: Lungs: take in oxygen, remove carbon dioxide
teach.note: Show a labelled body diagram. Ask pupils to point to where each organ is on themselves.

teach.heading: Plant organs
teach.note: Show a whole plant photo. Ask: 'Which plant organ is like our intestines?' (Roots absorb; leaves make food.)

teach.heading: Organs working together
teach.note: Trace oxygen from air to a muscle cell.

teach.heading: Location mix-ups
bullets: The heart is near the centre of the chest, slightly left
teach.note: Common error: pupils place the stomach behind the belly button and the heart on the far left.

misconception.wrong: The heart is on the far left of the chest
misconception.right: It sits near the centre, tilted slightly to the left

teach.heading: Check: function
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which organ removes urea from the blood?
check.why: Kidneys filter blood and make urine containing urea. The liver makes urea; lungs remove carbon dioxide.

practice: Label five organs on a body outline
Match plant organs to functions
Which organ is used for sensitivity?
independent: Core: Complete a table of eight organs (human and plant), their functions and life processes
Extend: Explain how the stomach, intestines and heart work together to get energy to a leg muscle
Stretch: Research one organ transplant (e.g. kidney). Explain why a person can live with one kidney but not without a heart.
exit: What is an organ?
Which plant organ makes food?
Name two organs involved in respiration.
lessons.homework: Draw and label a plant and a human body with five organs each and one function per organ.
lessons.send: Support: labelled diagrams to complete. EAL: organ word mat with pictures. Stretch: transplant research.

lessons.title: Using a microscope
lessons.bigQuestion: How did a microscope change what we think living things are made of?
objectives: Name the parts of a light microscope and their functions
Describe how to focus a microscope safely
successCriteria: Label the parts of a microscope
Describe the steps to view a slide, in order
Calculate magnification and explain why we start on the lowest power
lessons.crossCurricular: History: Robert Hooke and Antonie van Leeuwenhoek; Maths: multiplication and scale
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the hidden world in creation (Surah Al-Haqqah 69:38–39, 'what you see and what you do not see')

keywords.def: an instrument that makes small objects look bigger
how many times bigger an image is than the real object
the lens close to the specimen
the lens you look through
adjust until the image is sharp

starter: Name a plant organ and its job

teach.heading: Parts of a microscope
teach.note: Show a labelled photo; if you have a microscope at home, show it on camera. Ask pupils to point and name.

head: Part
Job
rows: big movements to find the image

teach.heading: Focusing safely
bullets: Look from the side as you move the lens down
Focus by moving the lens away from the slide
teach.note: Explain why: you could crack the slide or lens.

model.problem: Put the steps in order to view onion cells
steps: Clip the slide onto the stage over the hole
Select the lowest-power objective (×4)
Watching from the side, lower the lens close to the slide
Look through the eyepiece and focus upwards with the coarse focus
Sharpen with fine focus, then switch to a higher power
model.answer: Low power first, focus away from the slide

teach.heading: Total magnification
teach.note: Practise: eyepiece ×10, objectives ×4, ×10, ×40 → ×40, ×100, ×400.

teach.heading: Check: magnification
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: An eyepiece is ×15 and the objective is ×10. What is the total magnification?
check.why: 15 × 10 = 150. A adds the lenses instead of multiplying.

practice: Name the part you look through
Why do you start on the lowest power?
Total magnification with ×10 eyepiece and ×4 objective?
independent: Core: Write instructions, in order, for a Year 6 pupil to focus a microscope
Extend: Hooke saw cork cells at about ×50. Using an eyepiece of ×10, which objective would give this? What problem would there be?
Stretch: Explain why a light microscope cannot show the inside of a virus, using the idea of magnification and resolution.
exit: Which focus knob makes big movements?
Total magnification of ×10 and ×40?
Why look from the side when lowering the lens?
lessons.homework: Watch the teacher's video of onion cells under a microscope (or use a free virtual microscope) and sketch what you see at two magnifications.
lessons.send: Support: labelled diagram and step cards to order. Stretch: resolution and electron microscopes.

lessons.title: Animal and plant cells
lessons.bigQuestion: Why do plant cells need parts that animal cells do not?
objectives: Identify the parts of animal and plant cells
Describe the function of each part
successCriteria: Label nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane and mitochondria
Label and explain the extra plant cell parts
Explain why plant cells have a cell wall, chloroplasts and a vacuole
lessons.crossCurricular: Art: scientific drawing; Geography: plants and food chains
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the design and order in the smallest parts of living things

keywords.def: controls the cell and contains genetic material
controls what goes in and out of the cell
jelly where most chemical reactions happen
where respiration releases energy
where photosynthesis happens; contains chlorophyll

starter: Name two parts of a microscope
What is the smallest unit of life?
What do plants make in their leaves?

teach.heading: Parts in both cells
teach.note: Use an analogy: the cell is a school. Nucleus = head teacher's office; membrane = the gate; mitochondria = the canteen giving energy.

teach.heading: Extra parts in plant cells
bullets: Permanent vacuole: cell sap keeps the cell firm
teach.note: Ask: 'Why don't animals need a cell wall?' (Skeletons support us; we move.)

teach.heading: Wall versus membrane
bullets: The wall is outside the membrane
teach.note: A common exam slip.

misconception.wrong: Plant cells have a cell wall instead of a membrane
misconception.right: Plant cells have a cell wall AND a cell membrane

teach.heading: Not every plant cell is green
bullets: No light underground, so no photosynthesis
teach.note: Answer part of the big question: parts depend on the cell's job.

teach.heading: Check: plant or animal?
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A cell has a nucleus, membrane, cytoplasm and mitochondria but no wall. It is…
check.why: No cell wall, so it is an animal cell. Root cells lack chloroplasts but still have a wall.

practice: Label an animal cell diagram
Label a plant cell diagram
Name the part where respiration happens
independent: Core: Draw and label a plant and an animal cell using a sharp pencil, with a function for each label
Extend: Write a table of similarities and differences between plant and animal cells
Stretch: Explain why a cell from an onion bulb has no chloroplasts but a cell from an onion leaf does.
exit: What does the nucleus do?
Name one part only found in plant cells.
Where does photosynthesis happen?
lessons.homework: Make a model or annotated drawing of a plant cell from household items (photo to upload), labelling each part.
lessons.send: Support: labelled diagrams with word bank. EAL: cell-part cards. Stretch: specialised plant cells.

lessons.title: Specialised cells
lessons.bigQuestion: Why doesn't the body use one kind of cell for everything?
objectives: Describe examples of specialised animal and plant cells
Explain how their features suit their functions
successCriteria: Name five specialised cells and their jobs
Explain one adaptation of each
Explain why a specialised cell cannot do every job
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: muscle and nerve cells in movement; DT: form follows function
lessons.smsc: Social: like a community, different members with different roles work together

keywords.def: a cell with features suited to a particular job
a feature that helps something do its job or survive
the shape and parts of something
the job it does

starter: Name one part in both animal and plant cells
Which plant cells have no chloroplasts?

teach.heading: Shape fits the job
teach.note: Introduce with the big question. Like a school: teachers, cooks and cleaners all needed.

teach.heading: Specialised cells
bullets: Learn the cell, its job and one key feature
teach.note: Go through each with a picture.

head: Cell
Job
Adaptation
rows: no nucleus, more room for haemoglobin
long hair gives a big surface area

teach.heading: Explaining an adaptation
bullets: Feature → what it does → why that helps
teach.note: Model the sentence structure.

model.problem: Explain how a root hair cell is adapted to absorb water
steps: Feature: it has a long hair-like projection
Effect: this increases the surface area
Benefit: more water can be absorbed from the soil quickly
model.answer: Long projection → bigger surface area → faster water absorption

teach.heading: Mitochondria and energy
bullets: Cells that need lots of energy have many mitochondria
teach.note: Sperm and muscle cells. Ask why.

misconception.right: Mitochondria release energy from glucose in respiration

teach.heading: Check: adaptation
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Why does a red blood cell have no nucleus?
options: To make room for more haemoglobin to carry oxygen
check.why: Without a nucleus there is more space for haemoglobin, so more oxygen can be carried.

practice: Which cell has a tail?
Which plant cell has the most chloroplasts?
Give one adaptation of a nerve cell
independent: Core: Complete feature → effect → benefit sentences for four specialised cells
Extend: Ciliated cells line the airways. Research and explain how their cilia help keep the lungs clean
Stretch: Design a 'new' specialised cell for a job (e.g. storing fat), with three adaptations and reasons.
exit: What is a specialised cell?
How is a palisade cell adapted?
Why does a sperm cell have many mitochondria?
lessons.homework: Make revision cards for five specialised cells: picture, job and adaptation.
lessons.send: Support: sentence frame (feature → effect → benefit). Stretch: stem cells and differentiation.

lessons.title: Unicellular organisms
lessons.bigQuestion: How can one single cell do everything a whole animal does?
objectives: Explain how a unicellular organism carries out life processes
successCriteria: Name two unicellular organisms
Explain how an amoeba or Euglena feeds, moves and reproduces
Compare the advantages of being unicellular and multicellular
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: plankton in oceans; Food technology: yeast in bread-making
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: wonder at tiny organisms that support all life on Earth

keywords.def: made of one cell
made of many cells
a unicellular organism that changes shape to move and feed
a unicellular organism with chloroplasts and a flagellum
splitting in two to reproduce

teach.heading: One cell, all seven processes
bullets: Each part of the cell does a job
teach.note: Answer the big question: different parts of the single cell take on the roles organs have in us.

teach.heading: Amoeba and Euglena
bullets: Amoeba: moves with pseudopods, engulfs food
Euglena: swims with a flagellum, photosynthesises
teach.note: Show short videos (teacher-shared).

teach.heading: Reproduction by splitting
bullets: Binary fission: one cell becomes two
teach.note: Some bacteria divide every 20 minutes. Model the growth.

model.problem: One bacterium divides every 20 minutes. How many after 2 hours?
steps: 2 hours = 120 minutes = 6 divisions
That is 2⁶

teach.heading: Simple does not mean unimportant
bullets: Plankton make much of Earth's oxygen
teach.note: Challenge the idea that single-celled life is less important.

misconception.wrong: Unicellular organisms are all harmful germs
misconception.right: Many are useful: yeast, plankton, gut bacteria

teach.heading: Check: unicellular
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Why can Euglena make its own food?
check.why: Chloroplasts carry out photosynthesis. The flagellum moves it and the eyespot senses light.

practice: Name two unicellular organisms
How does an amoeba move?
What is binary fission?
independent: Core: Draw and label Euglena, linking each part to a life process
Extend: Explain why a unicellular organism can get oxygen by diffusion but a human cannot
Stretch: Yeast doubles every 90 minutes. How many cells grow from one cell in 9 hours? Why does growth slow down in real life?
exit: What does unicellular mean?
How does an amoeba feed?
Give one useful unicellular organism.
lessons.homework: Bake bread or watch a video of dough rising, and explain what the yeast is doing using the words respiration and carbon dioxide.
lessons.send: Support: labelled diagrams. Stretch: surface area to volume ratio.

lessons.title: Tissues, organs and organ systems
lessons.bigQuestion: How are cells organised to build a whole person?
objectives: Give examples of tissues, organs and organ systems
Explain how organ systems work together
successCriteria: Put cell, tissue, organ, organ system and organism in order
Give an example at each level for animals and plants
Explain how two organ systems depend on each other
lessons.crossCurricular: PE: musculoskeletal system; Geography: systems thinking
lessons.smsc: Social: like a well-run community, every level depends on the others

keywords.def: a group of similar cells working together
different tissues working together for a job
organs working together for a major function
a whole living thing

starter: Name an organ in a plant

teach.heading: Levels of organisation
teach.note: Use a muscle example at every level.

teach.heading: Main organ systems
teach.note: Also skeletal, muscular, excretory and reproductive. Show a body map of each.

teach.heading: Plants have levels too
teach.note: Ask pupils to build the plant version themselves first.

teach.heading: Tissue or organ?
bullets: A tissue is one type of cell
teach.note: The stomach contains muscle, glandular and lining tissue.

misconception.right: The stomach is an organ made of several tissues

teach.heading: Check: levels
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Which list is in the correct order, smallest first?
check.why: Cells form tissues, tissues form organs, organs form systems. D swaps tissue and organ.

practice: Order: organ, cell, organism, tissue, organ system
Give an example of a tissue
Name two organs in the digestive system
independent: Core: Complete a levels-of-organisation diagram for a human and for a plant
Extend: Explain how the respiratory and circulatory systems work together during exercise
Stretch: Choose an organ system. Explain what would happen to the whole organism if one organ in it failed.
exit: What is a tissue?
Name the organ system that includes the heart.
Put in order: system, cell, organ.
lessons.homework: Create a poster showing the five levels of organisation with a human and a plant example at each level.
lessons.send: Support: picture cards to sequence. Stretch: research an organ system disease.

lessons.title: 7A review: cells to systems
lessons.bigQuestion: What are the three most important ideas in 7A, and why?
objectives: Identify and close gaps in understanding
successCriteria: Recall key facts on cells, microscopes and organisation
Answer application and calculation questions
Explain and correct misconceptions in worked answers
lessons.crossCurricular: English: writing extended answers; Maths: magnification calculations
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: muhasabah, reflecting honestly on what we know

keywords.def: bring knowledge back from memory
use knowledge in a new situation
give reasons for something
say what something is like or what happens

starter: What does MRS GREN stand for?
Name two parts only in plant cells

teach.heading: Big ideas of 7A
bullets: All living things are made of cells
teach.note: Ask pupils to rank the three ideas by importance and justify.

teach.heading: Describe or explain?
teach.note: Model a 4-mark answer.

model.problem: Explain how a palisade cell is adapted for photosynthesis (3 marks)
steps: It contains many chloroplasts
Chloroplasts contain chlorophyll, which absorbs light
More chloroplasts means more photosynthesis, so more food is made
model.answer: Feature + how it works + why it helps

teach.heading: Common 7A errors
teach.note: Pupils correct each.

teach.heading: Check: apply
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A cell has a cell wall and vacuole but no chloroplasts. Where is it most likely from?
check.why: Plant cell (wall, vacuole) without chloroplasts: no light underground, so a root.

practice: Label a microscope
Label a plant cell
Name a specialised cell and its adaptation
independent: Core: 7A review quiz (15 marks): cells, microscope, organisation
Extend: Two extended answers: compare plant and animal cells (4 marks); explain how organ systems work together (4 marks)
Stretch: Data question: use magnification = image size ÷ real size to find the real size of a cell 5 mm wide in an image at ×500.
exit: One thing I'm confident about in 7A
One thing I need to revise
Write one question for a partner
lessons.homework: Revise 7A using your revision cards; complete the 7A end-of-unit check online.
lessons.send: Support: word bank and diagrams. Stretch: magnification formula with unit conversion.

lessons.title: Pure substances and mixtures
lessons.bigQuestion: Is the water in your tap 'pure'?
objectives: Use melting point to test purity
successCriteria: Classify materials as pure substances or mixtures
Explain the scientific meaning of 'pure'
Use melting-point data to decide whether a sample is pure
lessons.crossCurricular: Islamic Studies: purity (taharah) · compare the everyday and scientific meanings; Food tech: ingredients
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: the different meanings of purity in faith and science

keywords.def: contains only one substance
two or more substances mixed but not chemically joined
the temperature at which a solid melts
an unwanted substance in a mixture

starter: Is air one substance or many?
At what temperature does pure water boil?
Name a substance that dissolves in water

teach.heading: Everyday vs scientific 'pure'
bullets: Adverts: 'pure orange juice' means nothing added
teach.note: Answer the big question: tap water contains dissolved minerals and chlorine, so it is a mixture.

teach.heading: Testing purity
bullets: Pure substances melt at one exact temperature
teach.note: Show melting point data.

teach.heading: Mixed up meanings
bullets: Natural is not the same as pure
teach.note: Spring water is natural but a mixture.

misconception.right: It contains dissolved minerals, so it is a mixture

teach.heading: Check: pure?
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: A solid melts between 115 °C and 121 °C. What does this tell you?
check.why: Pure substances melt at a sharp, single temperature. A range means impurities are present.

practice: Classify: steel, salt, air, carbon dioxide, milk
What does 'pure' mean in science?
A sample melts at exactly 79 °C. Is it pure?
independent: Core: Sort twelve materials into pure and mixtures, with a reason for three
Extend: Explain why adding salt to icy roads helps them melt, using the idea of melting point
Stretch: A company claims its paracetamol is pure. Design a test using melting point and explain what result would support their claim (pure paracetamol melts at about 169 °C).
exit: Define a mixture.
Is sea water pure?
How can melting point show if a substance is pure?
lessons.homework: Find five labels at home that use the word 'pure' and decide whether each product is scientifically pure.
lessons.send: Support: picture sorting cards. Stretch: melting-point graphs.

lessons.title: Solutions and solubility
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does the sugar go when it 'disappears' in tea?
objectives: Use the words solute, solvent, solution and soluble
successCriteria: Use the four key words correctly
Explain dissolving and conservation of mass with particles
Interpret a solubility table or graph
lessons.crossCurricular: Maths: reading graphs; Food tech: making drinks and syrups
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: nothing truly disappears; mass is conserved

keywords.def: the substance that dissolves
the liquid that does the dissolving
a mixture of a solute dissolved in a solvent
able to dissolve
no more solute can dissolve

starter: Name something that does not dissolve in water

teach.heading: The words
teach.note: Quick-fire: salt water, coffee, squash. Pupils identify each word.

teach.heading: Particles explain dissolving
bullets: Solute particles spread out between solvent particles
They are too small to see
teach.note: Answer the big question. Show 100 g water + 10 g sugar = 110 g solution on a scale (video or demo).

model.problem: 50 g salt dissolves in 200 g water. What is the mass of the solution?
steps: Mass is conserved: no particles are lost
Solution = solute + solvent

teach.heading: Dissolving vs melting
bullets: Melting needs heat and one substance
teach.note: Very common error.

misconception.right: Sugar dissolves in tea; it would melt only if heated alone to about 186 °C

teach.heading: Solubility and temperature
bullets: Solubility: grams that dissolve in 100 g of water
For most solids it increases with temperature
teach.note: Show data for potassium nitrate: about 32 g at 20 °C, about 110 g at 60 °C (per 100 g water).

teach.heading: Check: words
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: In salty water, what is the solvent?
check.why: Water does the dissolving. Salt is the solute; salty water is the solution.

practice: Name the solute, solvent and solution in coffee
20 g of sugar in 150 g of water: mass of solution?
Insoluble or soluble: sand, salt, chalk, sugar?
independent: Core: Use the four keywords in sentences describing making squash
Extend: Use the KNO₃ table: how much more dissolves at 60 °C than at 20 °C? What happens when a saturated solution at 60 °C cools?
Stretch: Plan a fair test to find whether temperature affects how fast sugar dissolves. Name the independent, dependent and control variables.
exit: What is a solute?
Why does the mass not change when sugar dissolves?
Does solubility of most solids increase or decrease with temperature?
lessons.homework: At home, test how many teaspoons of sugar dissolve in a cup of cold water and a cup of warm water (with permission). Record and explain the result.
lessons.send: Support: word cards with pictures. Stretch: solubility curves.

lessons.title: Filtration
lessons.bigQuestion: How can a piece of paper separate sand from water?
objectives: Explain which mixtures filtration can and cannot separate
successCriteria: Describe the filtration method
Label residue and filtrate
Explain why filtration cannot remove dissolved salt
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: water treatment and access to clean water; DT: filters in products
lessons.smsc: Moral: the right to clean water; charity water projects (sadaqah jariyah)

keywords.def: separating an insoluble solid from a liquid using a filter
the solid left in the filter paper
the liquid that passes through the filter
does not dissolve

starter: What is the mass of a solution of 10 g salt in 90 g water?

teach.heading: How filtration works
bullets: Water and dissolved particles pass through
teach.note: Show the teacher's demo video: muddy water through a funnel and filter paper.

teach.heading: The method
bullets: Fold filter paper into a cone
Place in funnel over a beaker
teach.note: Home version: coffee filter or kitchen paper in a funnel over a jar, filtering sandy water.

model.problem: Separate sand from a mixture of sand and water
steps: Fold filter paper into a cone and place in a funnel
Stand the funnel in a beaker
Pour the mixture slowly into the cone
Sand stays in the paper; water collects below

teach.heading: What filtration cannot do
teach.note: Ask: 'Would filtering sea water make it drinkable?' No.

misconception.wrong: Filtering sea water removes the salt
misconception.right: Dissolved salt passes through the filter

teach.heading: Check: filtration
teach.note: Show me on 3.

check.q: Chalk and water are filtered. What is the filtrate?
check.why: The filtrate is the liquid that passes through. Chalk is insoluble and stays as the residue.

practice: Label a filtration diagram
Name the residue when filtering sand and water
Could you separate sugar from water by filtering?
independent: Core: Write a step-by-step method for filtering muddy water, with a labelled diagram
Extend: Explain how a water treatment works uses filtration through sand and gravel beds
Stretch: A mixture contains sand, salt and water. Which can filtration separate? What could you do next to get dry salt?
exit: What is the residue?
Why does salt pass through filter paper?
Name one use of filtration in real life.

lessons.title: Evaporation and crystallisation
objectives: Describe how evaporation separates a dissolved solid from a solution
Explain how crystallisation makes larger crystals
successCriteria: Describe evaporating a salt solution
Explain why slow cooling makes bigger crystals
Choose the right method and justify it
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: salt pans and coastal industries; History: the salt trade
lessons.smsc: Cultural: salt production around the world, from Cheshire to the Dead Sea

keywords.def: a liquid turning into a gas below its boiling point
forming crystals as a solution cools or evaporates slowly
a dish used to evaporate solutions
a solid with a regular shape

starter: Can filtering remove salt from water?
What happens to puddles on a sunny day?

teach.heading: Evaporation
teach.note: Answer the big question: sea water is let into shallow pans and the Sun evaporates the water.

teach.heading: Crystallisation
bullets: Heat until about half the water has gone
teach.note: Show teacher demo or video of copper sulfate crystals.

model.problem: Make pure copper sulfate crystals from its solution
steps: Heat the solution in an evaporating basin
Stop when crystals start to form at the edge
Leave somewhere warm to cool slowly
